report:
Conclusion: the claim is **supported for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk**, not as a blanket statement for all women.

The pivotal evidence is ACTIVE, an 18‑month randomized trial of 2,463 postmenopausal women: daily abaloparatide 80 µg cut new vertebral fractures versus placebo by about 86% (0.58% vs 4.22%; RR ≈0.14; absolute reduction ≈3.6 percentage points, NNT ≈28) and also reduced nonvertebral fractures (HR ≈0.57) (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640). FDA labeling reflects this: Tymlos is indicated for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high risk for fracture and states it reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf). Durability is supported by ACTIVExtend, where abaloparatide followed by alendronate maintained fracture-risk reduction (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7112966/), and a network meta-analysis found benefit versus placebo and some comparators (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-019-04947-2).

Caveats: use is generally limited to high-risk patients; labels warn about osteosarcoma findings in rats, hypercalcemia, and orthostatic hypotension, and cumulative PTH-analog exposure is typically restricted. Evidence is strongest for vertebral fracture reduction over 18 months, with sequencing to antiresorptive therapy afterward.
